[EFFECT]
Humidity has a non-monotonic, three-part effect on predicted hourly bike demand. At extremely low humidity (below about 10%, which is very rare in the data), the model heavily suppresses demand — likely reflecting unusual conditions. Across the typical mid-range of roughly 10%–65% relative humidity, the effect is broadly flat and mildly positive, with a gentle peak around 35–36% humidity. Above 65–70% relative humidity, demand is progressively pulled down, reaching a meaningful negative contribution at 100% humidity (roughly a 23–26% reduction in predicted rentals relative to the baseline).

[IMPORTANCE]
Humidity is the **5th most important** feature out of 9, with an importance score of 0.083. It sits just below month (0.086) and well behind the top three drivers — hour of day (0.889), temperature (0.253), and year (0.217) — meaning it has a moderate but secondary influence on demand.

[RECOMMENDATION]
When humidity climbs above about 65–70% (particularly on muggy or very damp days), the model anticipates noticeably fewer rentals, so staffing and bike redistribution resources can be scaled back on high-humidity days, while dry, comfortable days around 35–40% humidity represent the sweet spot for peak availability planning.
